documents.t: Production integrations with OpenWeatherMap rely on three architectural patterns: decoupled versioning between geographic lookup and atmospheric telemetry, coordinate-based request pipelines with tiered cache lifetimes, and server-side proxy mediation between client interfaces and https://api.openweathermap.org.

Although every free-tier endpoint is served from a single HTTPS gateway (https://api.openweathermap.org), OpenWeatherMap mounts domain capabilities under independently versioned path namespaces rather than a single monolithic version number: Decoupling Geocoding API 1.0 from Weather API 2.5 reflects a fundamental mismatch between geographic data and meteorological telemetry: Divergent rates of change: Administrative boundaries, postal codes, and multilingual place names (local_names) evolve on geopolitical timescales measured in months or years. Surface temperature, wind gusts, and radar precipitation shift every 10 minutes. Disambiguation before observation: Legacy string queries (GET /data/2.5/weather?q=Portland) force the weather engine to guess which "Portland" or "Springfield" a user meant without exposing alternative candidates. Extracting geocoding into /geo/1.0/direct returns up to 5 ranked candidates complete with name, state, country, lat, and lon, letting applications confirm the exact municipality before querying weather models. Independent schema and plan boundaries: Separating path prefixes also isolates free-tier 2.5 and 1.0 services from paid aggregation products such as One Call API 3.0 (/data/3.0/onecall), which operates on a separate per-call billing contract.

Modern OpenWeatherMap integrations treat lat and lon as the primary key for every weather request. When a user searches by city name or postal code, the application resolves human text into geographic coordinates first and queries Weather API 2.5 second—applying distinct cache lifetimes to each stage. Separating coordinate lookup from weather retrieval unlocks substantially higher cache hit ratios across your infrastructure: Service endpoint Upstream update cadence Recommended proxy TTL Architectural rationale /geo/1.0/direct, /geo/1.0/reverse, /geo/1.0/zip Static gazetteer updates 7–30 days (or persisted per saved user location) City coordinates do not move; once a user saves a city, persist its lat and lon so subsequent refreshes skip geocoding entirely. /data/2.5/weather Every 10 minutes 10 minutes (600 s) Matches OpenWeatherMap's observation assimilation cycle; rounding lat and lon to 3 decimal places (~110 m) coalesces nearby lookups onto one grid cell. /data/2.5/forecast Every 3 hours (synoptic runs) 30–60 minutes NWP forecast batches update on 3-hour schedules, allowing longer cache retention than current station snapshots.

During initial prototyping or inside developer tools (such as the interactive API playground, where you supply your own personal key in browser storage), calling https://api.openweathermap.org directly from client code validates connectivity with minimal setup. For multi-user production software, however, routing traffic through a backend-for-frontend (BFF) proxy—such as an Express route, FastAPI service, Next.js Route Handler, or serverless edge worker—is essential. Comparing the two topologies highlights three production failure modes that a BFF proxy eliminates: Production concern Direct browser or mobile calls Backend-for-frontend (BFF) proxy API key secrecy Bundling appid into frontend code (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_, or REACT_APP_ variables) exposes the raw credential in browser DevTools network logs and compiled JavaScript bundles, enabling quota theft. OPENWEATHER_API_KEY stays strictly in server-side environment variables or secret managers and never crosses the public network to clients. Browser CORS preflights Attaching custom HTTP headers (such as Authorization from global Axios or Fetch interceptors) triggers a browser OPTIONS preflight request that OpenWeatherMap rejects with a CORS failure. Server-to-server HTTPS calls are not governed by browser same-origin policy, eliminating preflight rejections and mixed-content blocks. Multi-user quota scaling Request volume scales linearly with visitor traffic: 200 concurrent readers viewing a homepage weather widget fire 200 requests/minute, breaching the 60 calls/minute free-tier limit and triggering 429 blocks. Request volume scales with unique cached locations rather than visitor count: 10,000 readers viewing London within 10 minutes trigger 1 upstream API call.

When your application queries the OpenWeatherMap API for a pair of coordinates, it doesn't read a standalone thermometer bolted to that exact street corner. Instead, the API serves values from a continuously updated global atmospheric grid synthesized from heterogeneous observational networks and physics-based prediction models. Understanding how OpenWeatherMap ingests, interpolates, and schedules those updates explains why several response fields—such as dt, main.temp_min, pop, and rain.3h—behave the way they do in production payloads.

No single observing network covers every square kilometer of Earth's surface, oceans, and upper atmosphere. OpenWeatherMap combines four complementary data streams inside its data assimilation pipeline: WMO and airport surface stations: Standardized SYNOP and METAR ground reports from World Meteorological Organization (WMO) member agencies (such as NOAA in the United States and the Met Office in the United Kingdom), airport weather stations, and tens of thousands of automated weather stations measuring 2 m air temperature, barometric pressure, dew point, and 10 m wind vectors. Doppler weather radar networks: Ground-based radar sweeps that measure hydrometeor reflectivity to track active rain bands, snowfall intensity, and convective storm cells at high spatial resolution. Geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites: Multispectral visible and infrared radiometry that observes cloud-top temperatures, cloud fraction (clouds.all), and atmospheric moisture over regions sparse in ground sensors, including oceans and mountain ranges. Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models: Global and regional physics simulations (incorporating feeds such as NOAA GFS and ECMWF) fused with statistical post-processing and machine learning assimilation models to reconcile sensor disagreements, reject faulty station spikes, and interpolate values between stations.

Because physical weather stations sit kilometers apart, OpenWeatherMap projects assimilated observations onto a continuous geographic grid. When a request supplies lat and lon, the model evaluates the containing grid cell alongside nearby reporting stations, weighted by distance, elevation, and observation freshness. This spatial design produces two behaviors that frequently surprise developers inspecting /data/2.5/weather: Nearby coordinates share readings: Two coordinates a few hundred meters apart inside the same neighborhood resolve against the same underlying station cluster and grid cell, returning identical temperature, pressure, and wind readings. main.temp_min and main.temp_max measure spatial spread, not 24-hour highs and lows: In /data/2.5/weather, temp_min and temp_max do not represent today's forecast daily minimum and maximum temperatures. Instead, they represent the instantaneous minimum and maximum temperatures currently observed across multiple stations or sub-grid points within a large metropolitan region (for example, cooler coastal neighborhoods versus warmer inland basins across Greater London or Los Angeles). Computing daily high and low temperatures In smaller cities, rural areas, or ocean coordinates governed by a single interpolated grid cell, main.temp, main.temp_min, and main.temp_max in /data/2.5/weather hold the exact same number. To display upcoming daily highs and lows on the free tier, aggregate the minimum and maximum values across the 3-hour intervals in the 5-day forecast endpoint.

documents.t: Every /data/2.5/weather payload includes a top-level dt integer representing a Unix UTC timestamp in seconds. That timestamp records when the meteorological observation or model assimilation snapshot was calculated—not when OpenWeatherMap's HTTP gateway serialized your JSON response. Between physical sensor sampling, telemetry transmission, automated quality control, and global grid recalculation, OpenWeatherMap refreshes current weather snapshots on a 10-minute cycle. As a result: dt routinely trails current UTC wall-clock time by up to 10 minutes: Receiving a payload at 14:28 UTC whose dt decodes to 14:20 UTC indicates normal pipeline operation rather than stale or broken data. Sub-minute polling yields duplicate readings: Querying /data/2.5/weather every few seconds for the same coordinates returns the exact same observation snapshot while consuming your 60 calls per minute quota. Aligning your backend cache time-to-live (TTL) to 10 minutes (600 s) matches upstream model freshness without sacrificing accuracy.

documents.t: Unlike current observations, medium-range weather prediction solves coupled differential equations across the global atmosphere on scheduled batch cycles. The /data/2.5/forecast endpoint exposes 5 days of predictions divided into 40 intervals of 3 hours each, aligned to the 8 standard WMO synoptic UTC hours: Synoptic window (UTC) Coverage period (UTC) Steps per 24-hour UTC day 00:00, 03:00, 06:00, 09:00 Midnight through noon UTC in 3-hour increments Steps 1–4 12:00, 15:00, 18:00, 21:00 Noon through midnight UTC in 3-hour increments Steps 5–8 Regardless of whether you query Tokyo (UTC+9), London (UTC+0 or UTC+1), or New York (UTC-5 or UTC-4), forecast step timestamps (list[].dt) always snap to those fixed UTC boundaries. Applications convert step labels into local civil time by adding city.timezone (the location's UTC offset in seconds) to each item's dt. Within each 3-hour forecast step, precipitation behavior is split across two complementary metrics: Probability of precipitation (pop): A floating-point ratio from 0 to 1 (0% to 100%) expressing the likelihood that measurable precipitation (0.1 mm or more of liquid equivalent) falls at the requested coordinate at any point during that 3-hour window. Accumulated volume (rain.3h and snow.3h): Expected precipitation depth in millimeters (mm) summed across the 3-hour interval. When the model predicts zero measurable rain or snow for a window, OpenWeatherMap omits the rain or snow object from that array element rather than emitting 0. Distinguishing probability from volume prevents misleading UI summaries. Widespread stratiform drizzle can produce high certainty with low volume ("pop": 0.92 alongside "rain": { "3h": 0.5 }), whereas scattered afternoon thunderstorms can carry moderate point probability with heavy localized accumulation ("pop": 0.4 alongside "rain": { "3h": 14.2 }).

OpenWeatherMap exposes a units query parameter (standard, metric, or imperial) on its weather and forecast endpoints, alongside timezone offsets and lang translations. However, units does not transform every physical measurement in the JSON payload—a design detail that causes subtle display bugs when applications assume units=imperial converts pressure to inches of mercury or rain to inches.

When a request omits the units parameter (or explicitly sets units=standard), OpenWeatherMap returns all temperature fields in Kelvin (K). A mild afternoon reading of 20 °C (68 °F) arrives as 293.15. OpenWeatherMap preserves Kelvin as the default for two reasons rooted in scientific computing: Thermodynamic SI consistency: Kelvin is the base unit of thermodynamic temperature in the International System of Units (SI), anchored at absolute zero (0 K, equivalent to -273.15 °C). Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models, radiative transfer formulas, and atmospheric gas-law equations compute directly in Kelvin because an absolute positive scale eliminates sign flips across the freezing point of water and keeps ratio math physically meaningful. Backward compatibility for data pipelines: Telemetry ingesters and scientific scripts built against Weather API 2.5 expect unparameterized requests to emit raw SI units (K for temperature and m/s for wind speed). For human-facing interfaces, you must either pass units=metric or units=imperial in the request URL, or convert temperatures in your presentation layer.

Only temperature and wind speed fields change when you switch units between standard, metric, and imperial. Every other physical measurement in OpenWeatherMap responses remains locked to a single SI or meteorological unit across all three modes.

Response fields standard (default) units=metric units=imperial main.temp, main.feels_like, main.temp_min, main.temp_max Kelvin (K) Celsius (°C) Fahrenheit (°F) wind.speed, wind.gust Meters per second (m/s) Meters per second (m/s) Miles per hour (mph) Metric wind speed uses meters per second Both standard and metric report wind.speed and wind.gust in meters per second (m/s), not kilometers per hour (km/h). To display km/h for metric locales such as Canada, Brazil, or mainland Europe, multiply the m/s value by 3.6.

When building localized interfaces—especially for United States (in, inHg, mi), aviation (kn), or metric road-weather (km/h) displays—apply standard deterministic conversions in application code: Source measurement Target unit Conversion formula Example Temperature (K) Celsius (°C) K - 273.15 288.55 K → 15.40 °C Temperature (°C) Fahrenheit (°F) (°C × 9 / 5) + 32 15.4 °C → 59.72 °F Wind speed (m/s) Kilometers per hour (km/h) m/s × 3.6 4.1 m/s → 14.76 km/h Wind speed (m/s) Miles per hour (mph) m/s × 2.23694 4.1 m/s → 9.17 mph Wind speed (m/s) Knots (kn) m/s × 1.94384 4.1 m/s → 7.97 kn Precipitation (mm) Inches (in) mm ÷ 25.4 2.54 mm → 0.10 in Pressure (hPa) Inches of mercury (inHg) hPa × 0.02953 1012 hPa → 29.88 inHg Visibility (m) Statute miles (mi) m ÷ 1609.344 10000 m → 6.21 mi

When designing an application that supports both Celsius and Fahrenheit users, you can choose between passing units dynamically to OpenWeatherMap or standardizing on a single canonical unit system inside your backend cache and converting values in the UI. Architectural dimension Server-side units query parameter Canonical backend metric + client UI conversion Backend cache efficiency Splits cache entries by unit (coord:51.507,-0.128:metric versus coord:51.507,-0.128:imperial), doubling upstream API calls for international traffic. Consolidates all visitors onto a single canonical cache key per location, cutting upstream API quota usage in half. UI unit-toggle responsiveness Switching between °C and °F requires an extra network round-trip (or storing duplicate payloads). Toggling between °C and °F updates the screen instantaneously in memory with zero network latency. Coverage of SI-only fields Still requires client conversion if imperial users expect precipitation in in, pressure in inHg, or visibility in mi. Centralizes all display formatting (°C/°F, km/h/mph, mm/in, hPa/inHg) in one pure formatting module. Best fit Single-locale CLI scripts, cron alerts, and stateless server-rendered views without unit toggles. Multi-user web and mobile applications backed by a shared caching proxy.

documents.t: Alongside physical units, OpenWeatherMap separates machine-invariant identifiers from human-localized presentation in timestamps and weather descriptions: UTC timestamps and timezone shifts: Every timestamp in the API (dt, sys.sunrise, sys.sunset, and list[].dt) is an integer count of Unix UTC seconds. To help format local civil clock times without an external time-zone database, /data/2.5/weather includes timezone (and /data/2.5/forecast includes city.timezone) representing the location's shift in seconds from UTC at the time of the request—such as -18000 (UTC-5) or 32400 (UTC+9), automatically reflecting active daylight saving time rules. Selective translation with lang: Passing lang (for example, lang=es, lang=fr, or lang=pt_br) translates only the human-readable weather[].description string (and localized place names where available). Structural fields—including JSON keys, numeric condition codes (weather[].id), and category groups (weather[].main, such as "Rain", "Snow", or "Clear")—remain in invariant English across every language so application icon mapping and conditional logic never break when you localize text.

Select curl, Node.js, or Python and run the request in the same terminal session where OPENWEATHER_API_KEY is set. curl Node.js Python Send a GET request to /data/2.5/weather with URL-encoded city and units=metric query parameters: macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) curl "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Rio%20de%20Janeiro&units=metric&appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" curl.exe "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=Rio%20de%20Janeiro&units=metric&appid=$env:OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" Save the following ES module as weather.mjs. Using the .mjs extension enables top-level await in Node.js 18 and later without requiring a package.json file: weather.mjs const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; if (!apiKey) { console.error( "Error: Missing OPENWEATHER_API_KEY environment variable. Set it before running weather.mjs." ); process.exit(1); } const url = new URL("https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather"); url.search = new URLSearchParams({ q: "Rio de Janeiro", units: "metric", appid: apiKey, }).toString(); const response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000), }); if (!response.ok) { const errorBody = await response.json().catch(() => null); const detail = errorBody?.message ?? response.statusText; console.error(`HTTP error ${response.status}: ${detail}`); process.exit(1); } const data = await response.json(); console.log( `${data.name}: ${data.main.temp}°C, ${data.weather[0].description} (humidity: ${data.main.humidity}%)` ); Run the script from your terminal: node weather.mjs Expected output: Rio de Janeiro: 28.5°C, clear sky (humidity: 70%) Save the following script as weather.py: weather.py import os import sys import requests api_key = os.environ.get("OPENWEATHER_API_KEY") if not api_key: print( "Error: Missing OPENWEATHER_API_KEY environment variable. Set it before running weather.py.", file=sys.stderr, ) sys.exit(1) response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather", params={ "q": "Rio de Janeiro", "units": "metric", "appid": api_key, }, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print( f"{data['name']}: {data['main']['temp']}°C, {data['weather'][0]['description']} (humidity: {data['main']['humidity']}%)" ) Run the script from your terminal: macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) python3 weather.py python weather.py Expected output: Rio de Janeiro: 28.5°C, clear sky (humidity: 70%)

A 200 OK call to /data/2.5/weather returns a JSON object containing geographic coordinates, weather condition codes, atmospheric readings, wind measurements, and metadata (abbreviated below): { "coord": { "lon": -43.2075, "lat": -22.9028 }, "weather": [ { "id": 800, "main": "Clear", "description": "clear sky", "icon": "01d" } ], "main": { "temp": 28.5, "feels_like": 30.8, "temp_min": 27.2, "temp_max": 29.4, "pressure": 1014, "humidity": 70 }, "wind": { "speed": 3.6, "deg": 120 }, "sys": { "country": "BR", "sunrise": 1715244180, "sunset": 1715284620 }, "name": "Rio de Janeiro", "cod": 200 } The table below summarizes the primary fields you'll work with in most applications: Field Type Description name string Matched city name ("Rio de Janeiro"). sys.country string Two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code ("BR"). main.temp number Current temperature in the requested unit system (°C for metric, °F for imperial, K for standard). main.feels_like number Perceived temperature accounting for humidity and wind. main.humidity integer Relative humidity percentage (0–100). weather[0].description string Weather condition summary ("clear sky"). wind.speed number Wind speed in m/s for metric and standard units, or mph for imperial units. cod integer Response status code (200 indicates success).

Every request to the OpenWeatherMap REST API authenticates with an API key passed in the appid query parameter. Follow these steps to create a free account, retrieve your key, store it in an environment variable, and verify that it's active.

Open the OpenWeatherMap sign-up page in your browser. Enter a username, your email address, and a password. Confirm that you meet the age requirement, accept the privacy policy and terms of service, and select Create Account. Open the verification email from OpenWeatherMap and select the confirmation link to activate your account.

Sign in to your OpenWeatherMap account. Select your username in the top navigation bar and select My API keys, or open https://home.openweathermap.org/api_keys directly on the My API keys page. Locate the Default key created automatically for your account, or enter a label such as local-dev under Create key and select Generate to create a dedicated key. Copy the 32-character hexadecimal key string to your clipboard.
documents.s: Step 2: Copy or generate an API key

documents.t: Code samples and tutorials throughout this documentation read your key from the OPENWEATHER_API_KEY environment variable so credentials stay out of your source code. Set OPENWEATHER_API_KEY in your terminal session, replacing your_api_key with the 32-character key you copied. macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) export OPENWEATHER_API_KEY="your_api_key" To keep the variable available in future terminal windows, append the export line to ~/.zshrc (macOS and Zsh) or ~/.bashrc (Linux and Bash) and reload your shell configuration. $env:OPENWEATHER_API_KEY = "your_api_key" To persist the variable across future PowerShell sessions for your user account, run [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("OPENWEATHER_API_KEY", "your_api_key", "User") and open a new terminal window. Print the variable to confirm that your current terminal session recognizes it. macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) echo "$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" $env:OPENWEATHER_API_KEY Never commit API keys to Git Treat your API key like a password. Never hardcode it in application files or commit it to Git repositories. Load credentials from environment variables, and add .env files to .gitignore before making your first commit.
documents.s: Step 3: Store your key in an environment variable

documents.t: New API keys typically activate within 10–15 minutes, though activation can take up to 2 hours. Send a test request for London using your OPENWEATHER_API_KEY environment variable. macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) curl "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=London&appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" curl.exe "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=London&appid=$env:OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" Compare the JSON response against the two possible states below.
documents.s: Step 4: Wait for activation and verify your key

documents.t: If your key is still activating—or if OPENWEATHER_API_KEY contains a typo—the API returns HTTP 401 with this JSON error payload: { "cod": 401, "message": "Invalid API key. See https://openweathermap.org/faq#error401 for more info." } Confirm that OPENWEATHER_API_KEY matches the 32-character string on your My API keys page with no extra spaces, wait 10–15 minutes, and run the command again.

Once activation finishes, the endpoint returns a 200 OK weather payload (abbreviated below): { "coord": { "lon": -0.1257, "lat": 51.5085 }, "weather": [ { "id": 804, "main": "Clouds", "description": "overcast clouds", "icon": "04d" } ], "main": { "temp": 285.15, "feels_like": 284.32, "humidity": 72 }, "name": "London", "cod": 200 } When you see "cod": 200, your API key is active and ready to use. Notice that "temp": 285.15 uses Kelvin by default when units is omitted, which you'll switch to Celsius on the next page.

Confirm that your local development environment has a command-line terminal and at least one supported runtime before starting. You don't need an OpenWeatherMap account or API key yet—you'll create both for free on the next page, Get your API key.

Terminal and curl: Preinstalled on macOS, most Linux distributions, and Windows 10 or later for sending HTTP requests directly from your shell. Language runtime (choose one or both for code examples and tutorials): Node.js 20 LTS or later: Recommended for the JavaScript examples and the Node.js dashboard tutorial. Node.js 18 and later include a built-in fetch implementation, so you don't need external HTTP packages. Download the LTS installer from the Node.js downloads page. Python 3.10 or later with requests: Recommended for the Python examples and the Python CLI tutorial. Download the latest installer from the Python downloads page. Code editor: Visual Studio Code or another text editor for authoring .mjs and .py scripts. REST fundamentals: Familiarity with running terminal commands, reading HTTP status codes, and inspecting JSON objects.
Run the commands for your operating system to confirm that curl and your preferred language runtime are available on your PATH.

macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) curl --version Expected output: curl 8.7.1 (x86_64-apple-darwin23.0) libcurl/8.7.1 ... In Windows PowerShell, curl is a built-in alias for Invoke-WebRequest. Run curl.exe explicitly to invoke the native curl binary: curl.exe --version Expected output: curl 8.9.1 (Windows) libcurl/8.9.1 Schannel WinIDN ...

If you plan to follow the JavaScript examples or the Node.js tutorial, verify your Node.js version: macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) node --version Expected output: v20.18.0 node --version Expected output: v20.18.0 Any version of v18.0.0 or later supports native fetch, and Node.js 20 LTS or later is recommended.

If you plan to follow the Python examples or the Python CLI tutorial, verify your Python version and install the requests package: macOS / Linux Windows (PowerShell) python3 --version python3 -m pip install requests Expected output: Python 3.12.6 Successfully installed ... requests-2.32.3 ... python --version python -m pip install requests Expected output: Python 3.12.6 Successfully installed ... requests-2.32.3 ... Isolate Python dependencies in projects For multi-file projects and tutorials, create a project-scoped virtual environment (.venv) before installing packages. The Build a weather CLI tool in Python tutorial walks through virtual environment setup step by step.

Use the q query parameter on /data/2.5/weather to fetch real-time weather observations for a named city when you don't yet have latitude and longitude coordinates. Prefer coordinates for production lookups OpenWeatherMap's built-in city-name lookup (q) is a legacy convenience feature that relies on internal ranking when multiple places share a name. For unambiguous production queries, resolve place names first and use geographic coordinates. Before running these examples, export your API key as OPENWEATHER_API_KEY. If you haven't created a key yet, see Get an API key.

Pass the city name in q, set units=metric to receive temperatures in Celsius, and include your key in appid: curl Node.js Python curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=Paris" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; async function getWeatherByCity(cityQuery) { const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: cityQuery, units: 'metric', appid: apiKey, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Weather request failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } return response.json(); } const weather = await getWeatherByCity('Paris'); console.log( `${weather.name} (${weather.sys.country}): ${weather.main.temp} °C, ${weather.weather[0].description}` ); import os import requests API_KEY = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"] WEATHER_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" def get_weather_by_city(city_query: str) -> dict: params = { "q": city_query, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY, } response = requests.get(WEATHER_URL, params=params, timeout=10) response.raise_for_status() return response.json() weather = get_weather_by_city("Paris") print( f"{weather['name']} ({weather['sys']['country']}): " f"{weather['main']['temp']} °C, {weather['weather'][0]['description']}" )

City names containing spaces or diacritics—such as Rio de Janeiro, New York, or São Paulo—must be percent-encoded in the query string. Avoid concatenating raw user input into URLs by hand; let your HTTP client serialize query parameters automatically: curl Node.js Python curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=Rio de Janeiro" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'Rio de Janeiro', units: 'metric', appid: process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Weather request failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); console.log(`${data.name} (${data.sys.country}): ${data.main.temp} °C`); import os import requests response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather", params={ "q": "Rio de Janeiro", "units": "metric", "appid": os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"], }, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print(f"{data['name']} ({data['sys']['country']}): {data['main']['temp']} °C")
Hundreds of municipalities worldwide share identical names. Append comma-separated ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes—and two-letter state codes for US cities—to target the exact jurisdiction you want.

Format q as {city},{country} to distinguish cities across countries, such as London,GB (United Kingdom) versus London,CA (Ontario, Canada): curl Node.js Python # London, United Kingdom curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=London,GB" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" # London, Ontario, Canada curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=London,CA" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; for (const query of ['London,GB', 'London,CA']) { const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: query, units: 'metric', appid: apiKey, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Request for ${query} failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); console.log( `${query} -> ${data.name}, ${data.sys.country} (${data.coord.lat}, ${data.coord.lon}): ${data.main.temp} °C` ); } import os import requests API_KEY = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"] for query in ("London,GB", "London,CA"): response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather", params={"q": query, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY}, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print( f"{query} -> {data['name']}, {data['sys']['country']} " f"({data['coord']['lat']}, {data['coord']['lon']}): {data['main']['temp']} °C" )

For cities in the United States, format q as {city},{state},{country}—for example, Portland,OR,US versus Portland,ME,US. Always include US as the third segment when passing a US state code. A two-part query treats the second segment as an ISO country code: Ontario,CA targets Ontario in Canada (CA), whereas Ontario,CA,US targets Ontario in California (CA,US). State codes apply only to the United States OpenWeatherMap supports {state} codes exclusively for US locations (US). For cities in Canada, Australia, Brazil, or any other country, pass {city},{country} without a state or province segment. curl Node.js Python # Portland, Oregon, United States curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=Portland,OR,US" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" # Portland, Maine, United States curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=Portland,ME,US" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; for (const query of ['Portland,OR,US', 'Portland,ME,US', 'Ontario,CA,US']) { const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: query, units: 'metric', appid: apiKey, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Request for ${query} failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); console.log( `${query} -> ${data.coord.lat}, ${data.coord.lon}: ${data.main.temp} °C` ); } import os import requests API_KEY = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"] for query in ("Portland,OR,US", "Portland,ME,US", "Ontario,CA,US"): response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather", params={"q": query, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY}, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print(f"{query} -> {data['coord']['lat']}, {data['coord']['lon']}: {data['main']['temp']} °C")

documents.t: Add the lang parameter to translate weather[0].description and the returned city name into the user's preferred language. Numeric condition codes (weather[0].id) and group names (weather[0].main) remain unchanged across languages, so branch your UI icon logic on weather[0].id rather than the translated description string: curl Node.js Python curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "q=Madrid,ES" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "lang=es" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'Madrid,ES', units: 'metric', lang: 'es', appid: process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Weather request failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); console.log({ city: data.name, conditionId: data.weather[0].id, group: data.weather[0].main, localizedDescription: data.weather[0].description, tempCelsius: data.main.temp, }); import os import requests response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather", params={ "q": "Madrid,ES", "units": "metric", "lang": "es", "appid": os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"], }, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print( { "city": data["name"], "condition_id": data["weather"][0]["id"], "group": data["weather"][0]["main"], "localized_description": data["weather"][0]["description"], "temp_celsius": data["main"]["temp"], } )

Use /data/2.5/forecast to retrieve up to 5 days (120 hours) of forecast data in 3-hour increments, cap the number of returned intervals with cnt, and roll 3-hour intervals up into local calendar-day summaries.

Query /data/2.5/forecast with lat and lon (recommended) or q along with units=metric. By default, the endpoint returns 40 forecast intervals (40 intervals × 3 hours = 120 hours): curl Node.js Python curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast" \ --data-urlencode "lat=35.6895" \ --data-urlencode "lon=139.6917" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: '35.6895', lon: '139.6917', units: 'metric', appid: process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Forecast request failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); console.log( `Received ${data.cnt} intervals for ${data.city.name} (${data.city.country})` ); import os import requests response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast", params={ "lat": 35.6895, "lon": 139.6917, "units": "metric", "appid": os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"], }, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() print(f"Received {data['cnt']} intervals for {data['city']['name']} ({data['city']['country']})") The response returns forecast blocks in list[] and location metadata—including city.timezone, the UTC offset in seconds—in city: { "cod": "200", "message": 0, "cnt": 40, "list": [ { "dt": 1746813600, "main": { "temp": 18.4, "temp_min": 17.9, "temp_max": 19.1, "humidity": 68 }, "weather": [ { "id": 500, "main": "Rain", "description": "light rain", "icon": "10n" } ], "pop": 0.42, "dt_txt": "2025-05-09 18:00:00" } ], "city": { "id": 1850147, "name": "Tokyo", "country": "JP", "timezone": 32400 } } For definitions of every field in list[] and city, see the 5-day forecast reference.

Pass cnt (1–40) when your application only displays upcoming hours. For example, setting cnt=8 returns the next 24 hours (8 intervals × 3 hours) and trims ~80% of the JSON payload: curl Node.js Python curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast" \ --data-urlencode "lat=35.6895" \ --data-urlencode "lon=139.6917" \ --data-urlencode "cnt=8" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: '35.6895', lon: '139.6917', cnt: '8', units: 'metric', appid: process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Forecast request failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); for (const slot of data.list) { console.log( `${slot.dt_txt} UTC -> ${slot.main.temp} °C (precipitation probability: ${Math.round(slot.pop * 100)}%)` ); } import os import requests response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast", params={ "lat": 35.6895, "lon": 139.6917, "cnt": 8, "units": "metric", "appid": os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"], }, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() for slot in data["list"]: pop_pct = round(slot["pop"] * 100) print(f"{slot['dt_txt']} UTC -> {slot['main']['temp']} °C (precipitation probability: {pop_pct}%)")

Don't group forecast intervals by item.dt_txt. The dt_txt field is always formatted in UTC, so splitting dt_txt assigns late-afternoon and evening intervals in non-UTC cities (such as Tokyo at UTC+9 or New York at UTC-4) to the wrong local calendar day. To build accurate daily summaries: Add data.city.timezone (seconds from UTC) to each interval's item.dt UTC Unix timestamp before formatting the YYYY-MM-DD date string in UTC. Track minTemp (item.main.temp_min), maxTemp (item.main.temp_max), and the most frequent item.weather[0].main condition across all intervals belonging to each local date. Because 40 three-hour intervals cover a rolling 120-hour window starting from the request time, the aggregated result spans 5–6 local calendar dates. The first and last dates usually contain fewer than 8 intervals because they represent partial days. Node.js Python const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; async function getDailyForecastSummary(lat, lon) { const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: String(lat), lon: String(lon), units: 'metric', appid: apiKey, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Forecast request failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const data = await response.json(); const timezoneOffsetSeconds = data.city.timezone; const dailyBuckets = new Map(); for (const item of data.list) { // Shift UTC epoch seconds by the target city's UTC offset before slicing YYYY-MM-DD const localDate = new Date((item.dt + timezoneOffsetSeconds) * 1000) .toISOString() .slice(0, 10); if (!dailyBuckets.has(localDate)) { dailyBuckets.set(localDate, { date: localDate, minTemp: Infinity, maxTemp: -Infinity, conditionCounts: new Map(), intervals: 0, }); } const bucket = dailyBuckets.get(localDate); bucket.minTemp = Math.min(bucket.minTemp, item.main.temp_min); bucket.maxTemp = Math.max(bucket.maxTemp, item.main.temp_max); bucket.intervals += 1; const condition = item.weather[0].main; bucket.conditionCounts.set( condition, (bucket.conditionCounts.get(condition) ?? 0) + 1 ); } return Array.from(dailyBuckets.values()).map((bucket) => { let dominantCondition = ''; let highestCount = 0; for (const [condition, count] of bucket.conditionCounts) { if (count > highestCount) { dominantCondition = condition; highestCount = count; } } return { date: bucket.date, minTemp: Number(bucket.minTemp.toFixed(1)), maxTemp: Number(bucket.maxTemp.toFixed(1)), dominantCondition, intervals: bucket.intervals, }; }); } const dailySummary = await getDailyForecastSummary(35.6895, 139.6917); console.log(JSON.stringify(dailySummary, null, 2)); from collections import Counter from datetime import datetime, timezone import json import os import requests API_KEY = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"] FORECAST_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast" def get_daily_forecast_summary(lat: float, lon: float) -> list[dict]: params = { "lat": lat, "lon": lon, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY, } response = requests.get(FORECAST_URL, params=params, timeout=10) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() timezone_offset_seconds = data["city"]["timezone"] daily_buckets: dict[str, dict] = {} for item in data["list"]: # Shift UTC epoch seconds by the target city's UTC offset before formatting YYYY-MM-DD local_date = datetime.fromtimestamp( item["dt"] + timezone_offset_seconds, tz=timezone.utc ).strftime("%Y-%m-%d") if local_date not in daily_buckets: daily_buckets[local_date] = { "min_temp": float("inf"), "max_temp": float("-inf"), "conditions": Counter(), "intervals": 0, } bucket = daily_buckets[local_date] bucket["min_temp"] = min(bucket["min_temp"], item["main"]["temp_min"]) bucket["max_temp"] = max(bucket["max_temp"], item["main"]["temp_max"]) bucket["conditions"][item["weather"][0]["main"]] += 1 bucket["intervals"] += 1 summaries = [] for date_str, bucket in daily_buckets.items(): dominant_condition = bucket["conditions"].most_common(1)[0][0] summaries.append( { "date": date_str, "minTemp": round(bucket["min_temp"], 1), "maxTemp": round(bucket["max_temp"], 1), "dominantCondition": dominant_condition, "intervals": bucket["intervals"], } ) return summaries daily_summary = get_daily_forecast_summary(35.6895, 139.6917) print(json.dumps(daily_summary, indent=2)) Running either script produces timezone-aligned daily high and low summaries across the 5–6 local calendar dates covered by the 120-hour window: [ { "date": "2025-05-10", "minTemp": 16.8, "maxTemp": 21.4, "dominantCondition": "Rain", "intervals": 7 }, { "date": "2025-05-11", "minTemp": 15.2, "maxTemp": 23.9, "dominantCondition": "Clear", "intervals": 8 }, { "date": "2025-05-12", "minTemp": 16.5, "maxTemp": 24.6, "dominantCondition": "Clouds", "intervals": 8 }, { "date": "2025-05-13", "minTemp": 17.1, "maxTemp": 22.8, "dominantCondition": "Clouds", "intervals": 8 }, { "date": "2025-05-14", "minTemp": 15.9, "maxTemp": 20.3, "dominantCondition": "Rain", "intervals": 8 }, { "date": "2025-05-15", "minTemp": 14.7, "maxTemp": 14.7, "dominantCondition": "Clear", "intervals": 1 } ] Filter partial boundary days when needed If your UI displays full-day cards only, check intervals >= 4 (or skip the final entry when intervals < 4) so a single midnight or early-morning interval doesn't misrepresent an entire day's high temperature.

Production weather integrations must distinguish permanent client errors (such as invalid credentials or unknown locations) from transient rate-limit and upstream gateway failures without crashing on unexpected payloads.

When OpenWeatherMap rejects a request at the application layer, it returns an HTTP error status alongside a JSON object containing cod and message: { "cod": "404", "message": "city not found" } Inconsistent status code types in payloads OpenWeatherMap returns cod as a string in some responses (such as "404") and as a number in others (such as 401). Always branch on the HTTP transport status (response.status in Node.js or response.status_code in Python) instead of comparing data.cod with strict type equality. Guard your JSON parser on non-2xx responses as well. Upstream load balancers and reverse proxies can return an HTML error document during 502 Bad Gateway or 503 Service Unavailable incidents. Calling an unguarded response.json() on an HTML body throws a syntax exception and masks the underlying HTTP status code.
documents.s: Check HTTP status codes before parsing JSON

documents.t: Only retry errors that can succeed on a subsequent attempt: Fail fast (zero retries) on 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, and 404 Not Found. Retrying permanent client errors wastes quota and delays feedback to the user. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 429 Too Many Requests, 500–599 server errors, and network timeouts. Because OpenWeatherMap omits the Retry-After header on 429 responses, rely on computed exponential backoff—while still honoring Retry-After if an intermediate proxy or gateway supplies it. Node.js Python const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; class WeatherApiError extends Error { constructor(message, { status, retryable }) { super(message); this.name = 'WeatherApiError'; this.status = status; this.retryable = retryable; } } const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); function computeBackoffMs(attempt, retryAfterHeader) { const retryAfterSeconds = Number(retryAfterHeader); if (Number.isFinite(retryAfterSeconds) && retryAfterSeconds > 0) { return retryAfterSeconds * 1000; } const baseMs = 1000 * 2 ** attempt; const jitterMs = Math.floor(Math.random() * 300); return baseMs + jitterMs; } export async function fetchWeatherWithRetry(lat, lon, { maxRetries = 3 } = {}) { const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: String(lat), lon: String(lon), units: 'metric', appid: apiKey, }); const url = `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`; for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= maxRetries; attempt += 1) { let response; try { response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) }); } catch (networkError) { if (attempt === maxRetries) { throw new WeatherApiError( `Network or timeout failure after ${maxRetries + 1} attempts: ${networkError.message}`, { status: null, retryable: true } ); } await delay(computeBackoffMs(attempt, null)); continue; } if (response.ok) { return response.json(); } // Parse body defensively in case a 502 or 503 proxy returns HTML instead of JSON const payload = await response.json().catch(() => ({})); const detail = typeof payload?.message === 'string' ? payload.message : response.statusText; if (response.status === 400) { throw new WeatherApiError(`Invalid request parameters: ${detail}`, { status: 400, retryable: false, }); } if (response.status === 401) { throw new WeatherApiError( `Authentication rejected (${detail}). Verify OPENWEATHER_API_KEY and key activation.`, { status: 401, retryable: false } ); } if (response.status === 404) { throw new WeatherApiError(`Requested location not found: ${detail}`, { status: 404, retryable: false, }); } const isRetryable = response.status === 429 || (response.status >= 500 && response.status <= 599); if (!isRetryable || attempt === maxRetries) { throw new WeatherApiError( `OpenWeatherMap HTTP ${response.status} (${detail})`, { status: response.status, retryable: isRetryable } ); } const waitMs = computeBackoffMs(attempt, response.headers.get('retry-after')); console.warn( `Transient HTTP ${response.status} on attempt ${attempt + 1}; retrying in ${waitMs} ms` ); await delay(waitMs); } } import os import random import time import requests API_KEY = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"] WEATHER_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" class WeatherApiError(Exception): def __init__(self, message: str, *, status: int | None, retryable: bool) -> None: super().__init__(message) self.status = status self.retryable = retryable def compute_backoff_seconds(attempt: int, retry_after_header: str | None) -> float: if retry_after_header is not None: try: parsed = float(retry_after_header) if parsed > 0: return parsed except ValueError: pass base_seconds = 1.0 * (2**attempt) jitter_seconds = random.uniform(0.0, 0.3) return base_seconds + jitter_seconds def fetch_weather_with_retry( lat: float, lon: float, *, max_retries: int = 3 ) -> dict: params = { "lat": lat, "lon": lon, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY, } for attempt in range(max_retries + 1): try: response = requests.get(WEATHER_URL, params=params, timeout=10) except requests.RequestException as exc: if attempt == max_retries: raise WeatherApiError( f"Network or timeout failure after {max_retries + 1} attempts: {exc}", status=None, retryable=True, ) from exc time.sleep(compute_backoff_seconds(attempt, None)) continue if 200 <= response.status_code <= 299: return response.json() # Parse body defensively in case a 502 or 503 proxy returns HTML instead of JSON try: payload = response.json() except ValueError: payload = {} detail = ( payload.get("message") if isinstance(payload, dict) and isinstance(payload.get("message"), str) else response.reason ) if response.status_code == 400: raise WeatherApiError( f"Invalid request parameters: {detail}", status=400, retryable=False, ) if response.status_code == 401: raise WeatherApiError( f"Authentication rejected ({detail}). Verify OPENWEATHER_API_KEY and key activation.", status=401, retryable=False, ) if response.status_code == 404: raise WeatherApiError( f"Requested location not found: {detail}", status=404, retryable=False, ) is_retryable = response.status_code == 429 or ( 500 <= response.status_code <= 599 ) if not is_retryable or attempt == max_retries: raise WeatherApiError( f"OpenWeatherMap HTTP {response.status_code} ({detail})", status=response.status_code, retryable=is_retryable, ) wait_seconds = compute_backoff_seconds( attempt, response.headers.get("Retry-After") ) print( f"Transient HTTP {response.status_code} on attempt {attempt + 1}; " f"retrying in {wait_seconds:.2f} s" ) time.sleep(wait_seconds) raise AssertionError("Unreachable retry loop exit")

documents.t: When upstream retries are exhausted, keep your interface usable instead of rendering a blank page: Serve stale-on-error cache entries: Retain the most recent observation for each location alongside its dt observation timestamp. If live retries fail, return the cached payload marked as stale and display an explicit timestamp banner such as "Showing conditions observed at 14:20 UTC." Differentiate user-recoverable errors from outages: Surface 404 Not Found as an inline prompt inviting the user to pick another city, while logging 401 Unauthorized and 500–599 failures to your server telemetry without exposing internal stack traces.

OpenWeatherMap's free tier enforces two quotas across all applications sharing an API key: a burst limit of 60 requests per minute and a monthly cap of 1,000,000 calls per month. Exceeding the burst limit returns 429 Too Many Requests. For tier-by-tier quota details, see Rate limits.

documents.t: Never call api.openweathermap.org directly from client browsers or mobile apps. In addition to exposing OPENWEATHER_API_KEY, client-side calls multiply traffic linearly with concurrent visitors: 120 visitors opening your homepage in the same minute trigger 120 upstream calls and trip 429 Too Many Requests. Route all client weather requests through a backend proxy configured with a 10-minute (600 s) cache time-to-live (TTL): Matches upstream model cadence: OpenWeatherMap refreshes station and model observations roughly every 10 minutes, so polling more frequently for the same location returns identical readings. See How weather data works for details on observation refresh cycles. Protects both quotas: Whether 10 or 10,000 users view London within a 10-minute window, your proxy sends 1 upstream call and serves the remaining requests from memory.

documents.t: A production caching proxy must enforce four safeguards: Validate OPENWEATHER_API_KEY at startup so misconfigured deployments fail immediately rather than returning 401 on live traffic. Normalize cache keys (city.trim().toLowerCase()) so "London", "london", and " london " share a single cache slot. Serialize query parameters safely (URLSearchParams in Node.js or params={...} in Python) so user-supplied :city path segments containing &, ?, or # cannot inject extra query parameters into the upstream URL. Cap maximum cache size (MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES = 500) and evict expired or least-recently-used entries so random or adversarial city queries cannot exhaust server heap memory. Node.js Python Install Express in an ES module project (Node.js 20+ provides native fetch and URLSearchParams): npm install express Save the following proxy as server.mjs and start it with node server.mjs: import express from 'express'; const API_KEY = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY?.trim(); if (!API_KEY) { throw new Error('Missing required environment variable: OPENWEATHER_API_KEY'); } const WEATHER_URL = 'https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather'; const CACHE_TTL_MS = 10 * 60 * 1000; const MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES = 500; const PORT = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000; const app = express(); const cache = new Map(); function getCachedEntry(key) { const entry = cache.get(key); if (!entry) { return null; } if (Date.now() - entry.timestamp >= CACHE_TTL_MS) { cache.delete(key); return null; } // Refresh Map insertion order so active locations remain cached cache.delete(key); cache.set(key, entry); return entry.data; } function setCachedEntry(key, data) { const now = Date.now(); if (cache.has(key)) { cache.delete(key); } else if (cache.size >= MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES) { for (const [existingKey, entry] of cache) { if (now - entry.timestamp >= CACHE_TTL_MS) { cache.delete(existingKey); } } if (cache.size >= MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES) { const oldestKey = cache.keys().next().value; cache.delete(oldestKey); } } cache.set(key, { timestamp: now, data }); } async function fetchCachedWeather(cacheKey, searchParams, res) { const cached = getCachedEntry(cacheKey); if (cached) { res.set('X-Cache', 'HIT'); return res.json(cached); } try { const upstream = await fetch(`${WEATHER_URL}?${searchParams}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000), }); const payload = await upstream.json().catch(() => ({})); if (!upstream.ok) { return res.status(upstream.status).json({ error: payload?.message ?? 'Upstream weather request failed', }); } setCachedEntry(cacheKey, payload); res.set('X-Cache', 'MISS'); return res.json(payload); } catch (error) { console.error(`Upstream fetch failed for ${cacheKey}: ${error.message}`); return res.status(502).json({ error: 'Upstream weather service unavailable' }); } } // Coordinate lookup route: GET /api/weather?lat=35.6895&lon=139.6917 app.get('/api/weather', async (req, res) => { const lat = Number(req.query.lat); const lon = Number(req.query.lon); if (!Number.isFinite(lat) || lat < -90 || lat > 90 || !Number.isFinite(lon) || lon < -180 || lon > 180) { return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Provide valid numeric lat (-90 to 90) and lon (-180 to 180) parameters.' }); } const latFixed = lat.toFixed(3); const lonFixed = lon.toFixed(3); const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: latFixed, lon: lonFixed, units: 'metric', appid: API_KEY, }); return fetchCachedWeather(`coord:${latFixed},${lonFixed}`, params, res); }); // City lookup route: GET /api/weather/:city app.get('/api/weather/:city', async (req, res) => { const normalizedCity = req.params.city.trim().toLowerCase(); if (!normalizedCity || normalizedCity.length > 120) { return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Provide a non-empty city query up to 120 characters.' }); } const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: normalizedCity, units: 'metric', appid: API_KEY, }); return fetchCachedWeather(`city:${normalizedCity}`, params, res); }); app.listen(PORT, () => { console.log(`Weather caching proxy listening on port ${PORT}`); }); Install FastAPI, Uvicorn, and HTTPX: pip install fastapi uvicorn httpx Save the following proxy as server.py and start it with uvicorn server:app --port 3000: from collections import OrderedDict from contextlib import asynccontextmanager import os import time from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query, Response import httpx API_KEY = os.environ.get("OPENWEATHER_API_KEY", "").strip() if not API_KEY: raise RuntimeError("Missing required environment variable: OPENWEATHER_API_KEY") WEATHER_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" CACHE_TTL_SECONDS = 600.0 MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES = 500 cache: OrderedDict[str, tuple[float, dict]] = OrderedDict() @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI): async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client: app.state.http_client = client yield app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan) def get_cached_entry(key: str) -> dict | None: entry = cache.get(key) if entry is None: return None timestamp, data = entry if time.monotonic() - timestamp >= CACHE_TTL_SECONDS: del cache[key] return None cache.move_to_end(key) return data def set_cached_entry(key: str, data: dict) -> None: now = time.monotonic() if key in cache: del cache[key] elif len(cache) >= MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES: expired_keys = [ k for k, (ts, _) in cache.items() if now - ts >= CACHE_TTL_SECONDS ] for k in expired_keys: del cache[k] if len(cache) >= MAX_CACHE_ENTRIES: cache.popitem(last=False) cache[key] = (now, data) async def fetch_cached_weather( cache_key: str, query_params: dict[str, str], response: Response ) -> dict: cached = get_cached_entry(cache_key) if cached is not None: response.headers["X-Cache"] = "HIT" return cached client: httpx.AsyncClient = app.state.http_client try: upstream = await client.get(WEATHER_URL, params=query_params) except httpx.HTTPError as exc: raise HTTPException( status_code=502, detail="Upstream weather service unavailable" ) from exc try: payload = upstream.json() except ValueError: payload = {} if upstream.status_code < 200 or upstream.status_code > 299: detail = ( payload.get("message") if isinstance(payload, dict) and isinstance(payload.get("message"), str) else "Upstream weather request failed" ) raise HTTPException(status_code=upstream.status_code, detail=detail) set_cached_entry(cache_key, payload) response.headers["X-Cache"] = "MISS" return payload @app.get("/api/weather") async def get_weather_by_coordinates( response: Response, lat: float = Query(..., ge=-90.0, le=90.0), lon: float = Query(..., ge=-180.0, le=180.0), ) -> dict: lat_fixed = f"{lat:.3f}" lon_fixed = f"{lon:.3f}" params = { "lat": lat_fixed, "lon": lon_fixed, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY, } return await fetch_cached_weather(f"coord:{lat_fixed},{lon_fixed}", params, response) @app.get("/api/weather/{city}") async def get_weather_by_city(city: str, response: Response) -> dict: normalized_city = city.strip().lower() if not normalized_city or len(normalized_city) > 120: raise HTTPException( status_code=400, detail="Provide a non-empty city query up to 120 characters.", ) params = { "q": normalized_city, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY, } return await fetch_cached_weather(f"city:{normalized_city}", params, response) Share cache state across horizontally scaled workers An in-process Map or OrderedDict isolates cache entries per process. If you run multiple container replicas or cluster workers behind a load balancer, store cached JSON payloads in Redis with SET key payload EX 600 so all replicas share a single 10-minute cache.

When a scheduled worker refreshes weather data for dozens or hundreds of saved locations, firing requests concurrently with Promise.all or a tight loop breaches the 60 requests per minute limit within seconds. Space sequential calls by 1,100 ms (~54 requests per minute), and combine pacing with automatic 429 Too Many Requests backoff in case another service sharing your API key consumes part of the per-minute budget: Node.js Python const API_KEY = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY?.trim(); if (!API_KEY) { throw new Error('Missing required environment variable: OPENWEATHER_API_KEY'); } const PACE_INTERVAL_MS = 1100; const MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES = 3; const delay = (ms) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); async function fetchLocationPaced(lat, lon) { const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: String(lat), lon: String(lon), units: 'metric', appid: API_KEY, }); for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES; attempt += 1) { const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (response.ok) { return response.json(); } if (response.status === 429 && attempt < MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES) { const retryHeader = Number(response.headers.get('retry-after')); const backoffMs = Number.isFinite(retryHeader) && retryHeader > 0 ? retryHeader * 1000 : 2000 * 2 ** attempt; console.warn(`Hit HTTP 429; pausing batch for ${backoffMs} ms`); await delay(backoffMs); continue; } throw new Error(`Request for (${lat}, ${lon}) failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } } async function syncLocationsBatch(locations) { const results = []; for (let i = 0; i < locations.length; i += 1) { const { label, lat, lon } = locations[i]; const data = await fetchLocationPaced(lat, lon); results.push({ label, tempCelsius: data.main.temp }); console.log(`[${i + 1}/${locations.length}] ${label}: ${data.main.temp} °C`); if (i < locations.length - 1) { await delay(PACE_INTERVAL_MS); } } return results; } await syncLocationsBatch([ { label: 'Tokyo', lat: 35.6895, lon: 139.6917 }, { label: 'London', lat: 51.5074, lon: -0.1278 }, { label: 'São Paulo', lat: -23.5505, lon: -46.6333 }, ]); import os import time import requests API_KEY = os.environ.get("OPENWEATHER_API_KEY", "").strip() if not API_KEY: raise RuntimeError("Missing required environment variable: OPENWEATHER_API_KEY") WEATHER_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" PACE_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 1.1 MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES = 3 def fetch_location_paced(lat: float, lon: float) -> dict: params = { "lat": lat, "lon": lon, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY, } for attempt in range(MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES + 1): response = requests.get(WEATHER_URL, params=params, timeout=10) if 200 <= response.status_code <= 299: return response.json() if response.status_code == 429 and attempt < MAX_RATE_LIMIT_RETRIES: retry_header = response.headers.get("Retry-After") backoff_seconds = 2.0 * (2**attempt) if retry_header is not None: try: parsed = float(retry_header) if parsed > 0: backoff_seconds = parsed except ValueError: pass print(f"Hit HTTP 429; pausing batch for {backoff_seconds:.1f} s") time.sleep(backoff_seconds) continue raise RuntimeError( f"Request for ({lat}, {lon}) failed with HTTP {response.status_code}" ) raise AssertionError("Unreachable retry loop exit") def sync_locations_batch(locations: list[dict]) -> list[dict]: results = [] for index, loc in enumerate(locations): data = fetch_location_paced(loc["lat"], loc["lon"]) results.append({"label": loc["label"], "temp_celsius": data["main"]["temp"]}) print(f"[{index + 1}/{len(locations)}] {loc['label']}: {data['main']['temp']} °C") if index < len(locations) - 1: time.sleep(PACE_INTERVAL_SECONDS) return results sync_locations_batch( [ {"label": "Tokyo", "lat": 35.6895, "lon": 139.6917}, {"label": "London", "lat": 51.5074, "lon": -0.1278}, {"label": "São Paulo", "lat": -23.5505, "lon": -46.6333}, ] )

Querying OpenWeatherMap endpoints with lat and lon eliminates duplicate-city ambiguity and uses OpenWeatherMap's primary coordinate lookup path instead of legacy name matching.

When a user searches for a city, resolve the text query to coordinates with Geocoding API 1.0 (/geo/1.0/direct) first, validate the response, and pass lat and lon to /data/2.5/weather: Always check both the HTTP status code and whether the parsed JSON body is a non-empty array before reading geoData[0]: An invalid API key returns HTTP 401 with a JSON object ({"cod": 401, ...}), where geoData.length is undefined. An unrecognized place name returns HTTP 200 with an empty JSON array ([]). curl Node.js Python # Step 1: Resolve "Paris,FR" to latitude and longitude curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct" \ --data-urlencode "q=Paris,FR" \ --data-urlencode "limit=1" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" # Step 2: Query current weather with the returned coordinates curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" \ --data-urlencode "lat=48.8588897" \ --data-urlencode "lon=2.3200410217200766" \ --data-urlencode "units=metric" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const apiKey = process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY; async function getWeatherForPlace(placeQuery) { const geoParams = new URLSearchParams({ q: placeQuery, limit: '1', appid: apiKey, }); const geoResponse = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct?${geoParams}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!geoResponse.ok) { throw new Error(`Geocoding request failed with HTTP ${geoResponse.status}`); } const geoData = await geoResponse.json(); if (!Array.isArray(geoData) || geoData.length === 0) { throw new Error(`No coordinates found for "${placeQuery}"`); } const { name, state, country, lat, lon } = geoData[0]; const weatherParams = new URLSearchParams({ lat: String(lat), lon: String(lon), units: 'metric', appid: apiKey, }); const weatherResponse = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?${weatherParams}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!weatherResponse.ok) { throw new Error(`Weather request failed with HTTP ${weatherResponse.status}`); } const weather = await weatherResponse.json(); return { resolvedName: [name, state, country].filter(Boolean).join(', '), lat, lon, tempCelsius: weather.main.temp, description: weather.weather[0].description, }; } const result = await getWeatherForPlace('Paris,FR'); console.log(result); import os import requests API_KEY = os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"] DIRECT_GEO_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct" WEATHER_URL = "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather" def get_weather_for_place(place_query: str) -> dict: geo_response = requests.get( DIRECT_GEO_URL, params={"q": place_query, "limit": 1, "appid": API_KEY}, timeout=10, ) geo_response.raise_for_status() geo_data = geo_response.json() if not isinstance(geo_data, list) or len(geo_data) == 0: raise ValueError(f'No coordinates found for "{place_query}"') match = geo_data[0] lat = match["lat"] lon = match["lon"] weather_response = requests.get( WEATHER_URL, params={"lat": lat, "lon": lon, "units": "metric", "appid": API_KEY}, timeout=10, ) weather_response.raise_for_status() weather = weather_response.json() label_parts = [match.get("name"), match.get("state"), match.get("country")] return { "resolved_name": ", ".join(part for part in label_parts if part), "lat": lat, "lon": lon, "temp_celsius": weather["main"]["temp"], "description": weather["weather"][0]["description"], } print(get_weather_for_place("Paris,FR")) Cache resolved coordinates aggressively City coordinates don't change. Cache /geo/1.0/direct lookups by normalized query string for days or weeks so repeat searches consume only a single weather API call.

documents.t: When your application starts from raw GPS or map-pin coordinates and needs a human-readable locality label, query the reverse geocoding endpoint (/geo/1.0/reverse) with lat, lon, and limit=1: curl Node.js Python curl --get "https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/reverse" \ --data-urlencode "lat=35.6895" \ --data-urlencode "lon=139.6917" \ --data-urlencode "limit=1" \ --data-urlencode "appid=$OPENWEATHER_API_KEY" const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: '35.6895', lon: '139.6917', limit: '1', appid: process.env.OPENWEATHER_API_KEY, }); const response = await fetch( `https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/reverse?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) } ); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Reverse geocoding failed with HTTP ${response.status}`); } const places = await response.json(); if (Array.isArray(places) && places.length > 0) { const { name, state, country } = places[0]; console.log([name, state, country].filter(Boolean).join(', ')); } import os import requests response = requests.get( "https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/reverse", params={ "lat": 35.6895, "lon": 139.6917, "limit": 1, "appid": os.environ["OPENWEATHER_API_KEY"], }, timeout=10, ) response.raise_for_status() places = response.json() if isinstance(places, list) and len(places) > 0: place = places[0] parts = [place.get("name"), place.get("state"), place.get("country")] print(", ".join(part for part in parts if part))

documents.t: In web applications, you can read the user's coordinates from the browser Geolocation API (navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition) without asking them to type a city name. Keep your API key on the server Never call api.openweathermap.org directly from client-side browser code. Any key bundled into frontend JavaScript or sent from browser network requests is visible to every visitor. Send lat and lon to your own backend endpoint, and attach OPENWEATHER_API_KEY on the server. Capture coordinates in the browser and forward them to your own backend route (/api/weather): function loadLocalWeather(onSuccess, onFallbackRequired) { if (!('geolocation' in navigator)) { onFallbackRequired('Browser geolocation is unavailable.'); return; } navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition( async (position) => { try { const params = new URLSearchParams({ lat: position.coords.latitude.toFixed(4), lon: position.coords.longitude.toFixed(4), }); // Send coordinates to your own backend proxy rather than OpenWeatherMap directly const response = await fetch(`/api/weather?${params}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000), }); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error(`Backend weather route returned HTTP ${response.status}`); } const weather = await response.json(); onSuccess(weather); } catch (error) { onFallbackRequired(error.message); } }, (geoError) => { onFallbackRequired(`Location permission declined or timed out (${geoError.message}).`); }, { enableHighAccuracy: false, timeout: 8000, maximumAge: 600000 } ); } Rounding latitude and longitude to 2–4 decimal places before calling /api/weather improves privacy and increases cache hit rates across nearby users. To build the /api/weather server route with bounded caching, see Set up rate limiting and caching. Provide a manual search fallback Users frequently decline browser location prompts. Pair geolocation with a city-search input backed by /geo/1.0/direct on your server so users can always select a location manually.

Welcome to the unofficial developer documentation for the OpenWeatherMap REST API, authored as a technical writing portfolio sample by Michel Silveira. This site guides you from your first authenticated 200 OK request to production-ready caching, coordinate resolution, and error recovery. Every page follows the Diátaxis framework so you can move directly to hands-on learning, task-oriented code recipes, exact endpoint schemas, or architectural mental models.

OpenWeatherMap's free tier requires no credit card and includes 60 calls per minute and 1,000,000 calls per month across two versioned REST services under https://api.openweathermap.org: Current weather (GET /data/2.5/weather): Near-real-time temperature, humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind vector, visibility, cloud cover, and precipitation observations refreshed every 10 minutes. 5-day forecast (GET /data/2.5/forecast): 40 forecast steps in 3-hour synoptic UTC intervals covering the next 5 days, including probability of precipitation (pop) and 3-hour rain or snow accumulation. Global geocoding (GET /geo/1.0/direct, /geo/1.0/reverse, and /geo/1.0/zip): Forward place-name search, reverse coordinate lookup, and postal-code resolution into exact latitude and longitude coordinates. Historical weather archives, extended 16-day daily forecasts, and One Call API 3.0 (/data/3.0/onecall) require separate paid billing plans and are not included in the free tier.
